analysis.one_liner: Orders regulators to impose strict limits on banks and hedge funds speculating in energy futures markets.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: referred to the House Agriculture Committee in June 2009, it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: In June 2009, gas prices had jumped more than a dollar a gallon in six months while U.S. oil inventories were at record highs and demand was falling—circumstances the bill said pointed to Wall Street speculation. The bill would have ordered the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the agency that polices futures markets, to immediately impose strict position limits on banks and hedge funds trading energy futures, break up firms that both forecast oil prices and trade oil derivatives, and close regulatory loopholes that let foreign exchanges sell U.S. energy trading to U.S. investors. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which oversees commodity futures, and never received any further action beyond a subcommittee referral a year later.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay gasoline, diesel, heating oil, and natural gas prices set in energy futures markets. The bill's premise was that when banks and hedge funds place large speculative bets, prices can detach from real supply and demand, and everyone who buys fuel or goods shipped by truck pays the difference. Airlines, trucking companies, and farmers who buy fuel would also benefit from prices that track the physical market.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone who buys gasoline and fuel

how_it_helps.text: The bill directed the CFTC to curb excessive speculation and eliminate price distortions in energy futures and swaps markets, so that prices reflect actual supply and demand rather than trading activity.
It would have immediately subjected bank holding companies trading energy futures to strict position limits, treating them as speculators rather than hedgers.
It required hedge funds trading energy futures to register with the CFTC and accept strict speculation limits, bringing previously unregulated players under federal oversight.
It ordered the CFTC to eliminate conflicts of interest where one entity predicts oil prices, operates oil assets like pipelines and storage, and trades oil derivatives at the same time.

It revoked the regulatory exemptions (no-action letters) that let foreign exchanges operating terminals in the United States sell trading in U.S. commodities to U.S. investors outside the strictest U.S. limits.

analysis.who_pays: Bank holding companies and hedge funds that profit from large speculative positions in energy futures would face strict position limits, registration requirements, and the loss of regulatory exemptions. Commodity exchanges and dealers that profit from high trading volume and from conflicts of interest between price forecasting, asset ownership, and derivatives trading would lose business.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and hedge funds betting on energy

drawbacks.text: The bill ordered the CFTC to act 'immediately'—imposing strict position limits on all bank holding companies and hedge funds and revoking existing no-action letters—without any study or phase-in, raising the risk of disrupting legitimate hedging by airlines, fuel distributors, and farmers who use energy futures to lock in costs.

The link between speculation and the 2009 gasoline price rise was contested: the bill cited record crude inventories and falling demand alongside rising prices as circumstantial evidence, but never proved how much of the price move was speculative rather than driven by expectations of economic recovery.

The conflict-of-interest provision, by forbidding one entity from simultaneously forecasting prices, operating oil assets, and trading derivatives, would have forced major financial firms to break up or restructure existing energy trading businesses.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was lower gasoline and heating bills if the bill's premise was right—that Wall Street speculation, not supply and demand, was pushing prices up; the bill's own findings cited record oil inventories, decade-low demand, and a 70% price jump at the same time [S3]. The cost was reduced liquidity in energy futures markets, which some economists argue can widen price spreads for hedgers like airlines and fuel distributors, and the risk that rigid position limits designed for one crisis become permanent obstacles in the next. The bill was also blunt: rather than writing new rules, it ordered the CFTC to act "immediately" across a range of complex markets, which would likely have produced litigation and uneven enforcement. On balance it was a consumer-protection measure whose main weakness was design, and it never got far enough for Congress to weigh any of this in the open.

outcome.mechanism: The House Agriculture Committee, where the bill was referred on the day it was introduced, never scheduled action on it, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: DeFazio introduced the bill on June 15, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Agriculture.
On June 22, 2010, a year later, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management—the last action ever taken on it.
The bill never reached the House floor and never received a vote of any kind before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Over the bill's entire 18-month lifespan, only one other member, Rep. Peter Welch of Vermont, signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and hedge funds trading energy futures kept their unrestricted position limits and regulatory exemptions, since nothing in the bill ever became law. Gasoline prices were set by the same markets the bill sought to change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and hedge funds trading energy futures

for.name: Rep. Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill directing the CFTC to impose strict position limits on banks and hedge funds trading energy futures and to close regulatory exemptions.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over commodity futures
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, referred it to a subcommittee a year later, and never reported it out or scheduled any markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never attracted enough support to test a party split: two Democrats sponsored it and no other member of either party signed on.

industries.industry: Investment banks and bank holding companies trading energy futures
industries.note: The bill would have reclassified any bank holding company trading energy futures as a speculator and imposed strict position limits, directly curtailing a profitable trading business. The cost, if the bill's premise held, would have been passed on to consumers only in the form of lower fuel prices.

Hedge funds trading energy futures would have had to register with the CFTC and accept strict speculation limits for the first time. Their unrestricted access to energy markets was the core target of the bill.

industries.industry: Commodity exchanges and energy derivatives dealers, including foreign exchanges with U.S. terminals
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated regulatory exemptions for foreign boards of trade selling U.S. commodity trading to U.S. investors and forced separation of price forecasting, asset operation, and derivatives trading within single firms. Losing those exemptions and conflicts meant less trading volume and fewer profitable structures.
